props.title: The Goodbye Girl

sections.content: The Goodbye Girl (1977) stands as one of Neil Simon's most charming romantic comedies, perfectly capturing the gritty-yet-hopeful mood of late 70s New York. Richard Dreyfuss's Oscar-winning performance as struggling actor Elliot Garfield crackles with the same intense energy he brought to Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977) that same year, but channeled into razor-sharp comedy. His chemistry with Marsha Mason feels genuine and earned, unlike the more formulaic romcoms that would dominate the 1980s like When Harry Met Sally (1989).

sections.content: The film exemplifies the more grounded, character-driven romantic comedies of the 1970s, sharing DNA with Annie Hall (1977) and Starting Over (1979). These films tackled real relationship struggles with wit and vulnerability rather than contrived meet-cutes. Simon's screenplay masterfully balances sharp dialogue with genuine emotional stakes, while Quinn Cummings as precocious daughter Lucy delivers one of cinema's least annoying child performances.

What sets The Goodbye Girl apart is its insider's view of the New York theater scene, predating similar showbiz relationship films like All That Jazz (1979) and Tootsie (1982). Elliot's disastrous turn as an "off-off-Broadway" Richard III becomes both a brilliant comedy set piece and a meditation on artistic integrity. The film's portrayal of struggling artists sharing cramped apartments remains relevant today. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Urban Romance

movies.title: The Turning Point
movies.slug: Two former ballerinas confront their life choices and rivalry while one's daughter enters the dance world

sections.content: While modern viewers might find some elements dated, the film's core themes about trust, career vs. relationship sacrifices, and single parenthood remain startlingly contemporary. It bridges the gap between the screwball comedies of classic Hollywood and the more naturalistic romantic films that would follow like Broadcast News (1987) and Moonstruck (1987). Director Herbert Ross, who also helmed Steel Magnolias (1989), brings a theatrical energy while keeping the emotional moments grounded.
